toc.title: The theory is not a prescription
The real benefit: a new narrative
What the new story can sound like
How to build it, in order

blocks.p: Are you struggling with shame, blame, or judgment? You might have been taught that you need to sit with the feelings or talk them out. But there's a simpler step you can take before going deeper and risking re-traumatization: putting together a newer, simpler, nonjudgmental and non-shaming narrative, based on the science of the Polyvagal Theory.

When people first get interested in the Polyvagal Theory, they're looking for answers, on a professional level or a personal level. There's a really good chance you're either on your own trauma recovery journey, or you're a professional helping somebody on theirs. I'll stick with the person on their personal journey.

You want to know what to do with your trauma. You want to know how to make change. You find this theory, and after learning it you see, or feel, or intuitively know that there's something here: some avenue for learning about this and then applying it to yourself.

You want to identify your stuck defensive state, and then climb the [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system) into your safety state. People are really drawn to Deb Dana's "home away from home" concept: "What's my stuck defensive state? Where do I fit on the polyvagal ladder?" So you want to learn, and apply, and build some insight. Lots of top-down, knowledge kind of stuff.

I completely get that. Of course you're looking for more information. And yes, the Polyvagal Theory can help you build insight into yourself, like what your stuck defensive state is, or how to access your safety state.

blocks.h: The theory is not a prescription

blocks.p: But the Polyvagal Theory is not a prescription. A lot of times we learn it and think, "Therefore I must..." do whatever. It's not that.
None of it is prescribed. None of it is set in stone. It's different for each of us. And the "what to do with it" is not super clear.

blocks.h: The real benefit: a new narrative

blocks.p: So here's the real benefit of learning the Polyvagal Theory, or at least the most immediate potential benefit, the way I understand it: you can apply it to yourself, and that has a potential lasting impact. It opens up the potential for you to create a new narrative for yourself. A new story of your past, sure, but also a new understanding of your present.
Before learning the Polyvagal Theory, you might have been looking at past events and blaming yourself. "Why didn't I do this?" "Why did I have to do that?"

There are always things to take responsibility for, and that's not what I'm talking about. Taking responsibility for your choices: fantastic, great job. What I mean is assigning blame to yourself when maybe it's not deserved, necessary, or functional. Accepting blame can even solidify a toxic environment or relationship, a system that doesn't need to be in place.

Saying, "I messed up, I can do better next time," is taking responsibility. That's fine. That's a lot different from a dysregulated cognition like, "It's my fault my parents got divorced when I was younger." If you still believe that, or believed it back then, it's probably not true. I don't think I've ever blamed the children for that. That's the kind of thing you might be able to build a new story around with the Polyvagal Theory: "My parents existed in a dysregulated state and were unable to stay together. It had nothing to do with me as a kid."

I can't go deeper into this for you in particular, so you'll need to discern what's responsibility and what's blame. For now, take this idea of building a new narrative and place it onto the pieces of blame you're putting on yourself that maybe you don't deserve.

blocks.h: What the new story can sound like

blocks.p: Along with that blame, you might be shaming and judging yourself as well. It might sound like, "I am such an idiot. Why do I always do this?" Or, "I knew it. I'm unlovable and not worth anything."
After learning the Polyvagal Theory and applying it to yourself, you might be more open to a new way of viewing the past, the present, and maybe even the future. You might be able to say:

ul: "I was stuck in a freeze state, and that's why I couldn't speak up for myself."
"I was so dysregulated and overwhelmed that I let my boundaries slip again."

blocks.p: That sounds like a lot less judgment to me. That sounds like someone who can look at things with a foundation of new knowledge, apply it to that context, and come away with a much less judgmental version of events.

You might also realize that the people in your life, even your parents, were working from their own stuck defensive states, and maybe they simply weren't able to care for you the way you needed, the way you deserved. Instead of blaming and judging and shaming them (and hey, maybe they deserved it all, I'll put that out there), you might be able to look at your life context and say, "I was surrounded by people who were in very dysregulated defensive states." And maybe that's still true now. Maybe these people are still in stuck defensive states and still unable to provide co-regulation, or connection, or safety for you.
Deb Dana put it this way when she was on the podcast:

q: We are story making beings, that's what we do as humans. I'd like the story to be based in the biology. What's your autonomic story, not what's your cognitive story.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana Interview: Story Follows State, Climbing the Ladder and Diagnosing (episode 29)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c)

blocks.h: How to build it, in order

blocks.p: Applying this to yourself and looking at the past can be very difficult. So here's the order I'd encourage.

ol: Let the learning settle. Before applying the polyvagal information to yourself, before attempting to recover from whatever traumatized state you're in, let it settle. Take your time with it. Learn it as deeply as you can. Read the original sources. And don't quite do anything with it yet. I know that's hard, because it's exciting and you want to start applying it. I can't tell you how long, but sit on it. Don't sit with your feelings quite yet. You might not be there. Sit with your learning.

Apply it to the present moment, not the past. Once you think you understand it well enough, apply that knowledge to yourself in the present moment. Not the past, not yet at least. It's really easy to go into past events and past relationships, but stay with the here and now as much as you can. Apply it with as much curiosity as you can, which means you're anchored in your safety state. From there, apply it to yourself in the present moment, as best you can handle it, and build that new narrative of yourself through the lens of the Polyvagal Theory.

Then, when you're ready, the past. Yes, we can apply this to the past as well. But you need to make sure you're ready for that. Then apply the polyvagal knowledge to those past contexts as much as you can handle. A little bit at a time is completely fine.

blocks.p: Don't answer these until you know you're ready to handle it and you're coming from curiosity. Use them for journaling if you like, or just think about them as you read. Maybe it's thirty seconds. Maybe you journal for fifteen minutes. It's up to you. Notice what you can handle and run with it if you're capable of doing so. If not, come back to it. That's completely fine too.
Apply them to whatever context you need to. I don't know your life. If you have something in mind that's tolerable, something you can handle, use these:

ol: How much access did you have to your safety state?
Was it realistic to be able to develop your safety state in that context, or to access it, or to use it?
How much access did other people have to their safety state? Were they able to provide co-regulation? Were they able to be empathetic and see that maybe you needed something else?
Is it possible that you had to exist in a defensive state in that context?
Is it possible you existed in a defensive state to get your needs met?
Do you think your body actually did its job by putting you into a defensive state in that context?
Do you think you had an impulse to connect with others in safety that maybe could not be returned by them?

blocks.p: For these prompts to really click, you have to have a clear understanding of the Polyvagal Theory and how it connects to trauma. If you're still learning and letting it settle, spend more time there. Once you really get it, let it settle, then apply it to yourself, and you'll be better able to give yourself that new, judgment-free and shame-free narrative.
